title: Grand Junction Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Grand Junction wells have a 20 ft median depth, but records range to 1,690 ft. See yields, water levels, permits, risks and costs.
h1: Grand Junction Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Grand Junction well records look shallow at first glance: the median reported depth is 20 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 28 feet. That does not mean every lot has an easy, inexpensive well. The records include wells as deep as 1,690 feet, and most named aquifers are unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than a single uniform groundwater source.

This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Grand Junction, including nearby Orchard Mesa, Redlands and Fruitvale. Use the statistics to screen a property, then have a Colorado well professional review the permit history, geology, water rights and proposed well location before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Grand Junction well depths vary sharply by ground conditions
sections.html:
The local depth profile is dominated by shallow records: 93% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Another 2% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 2% between 300 and 600 feet, and 3% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,690 feet.

For a driller's bid, the median is a useful starting point, not a guarantee. A site near shallow alluvial material may fit the local pattern, while fractured-bedrock conditions or an unusual permit area can require substantially more drilling. The aquifer records support that caution: 1,783 wells name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, compared with 75 alluvial wells and 6 Entrada wells.

sections.heading: What Grand Junction wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 44 records reporting pump yield, the median is 5.5 gallons per minute. The middle half spans 0.1 to 12.6 gallons per minute, so nearby wells can perform very differently. A yield test is more useful for a specific purchase than the regional median.

The low-yield share deserves attention: 39% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 2% are in the 1 to 5 gallon-per-minute range, 36% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 23% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the original well test and confirm the intended household, irrigation or livestock demand. A storage tank can help manage a slow well, but it does not create more groundwater.

sections.heading: Water levels near Grand Junction are shallow, not steadily falling
sections.html:
The 111 records with static water-level measurements show a median depth to water of 14 feet, with the middle half between 10 and 19 feet. That is useful for planning a pump setting, trenching and construction access, but a static level is not the same as a tested production rate.

The decade figures do not show a simple dropping water table. The median was 16 feet below surface in the 2000s, 10 feet in the 2010s, and 18 feet in the 2020s. Measurement locations, seasons, pumping and different well types can affect those comparisons. Check the actual neighboring logs rather than treating the regional series as a prediction for one lot.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity and heavy monitoring use
sections.html:
Grand Junction has 2,007 wells in Colorado DWR permit records, with 757 recorded as constructed and 1,141 reporting a total depth. The permit count rose from 10 in the 1950s to 523 in the 2010s; the 2020s already contain 303 permits, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

Use type matters when comparing nearby records. Monitoring wells account for 78% of the use mix, while domestic or household wells account for 4%, stock wells 1% and irrigation wells 2%. The most active named record holder is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 826 records. Da Smith Drilling Company has 22, and Layne, Christensen Co. has 12. Confirm who will perform current work and verify licensing before signing a contract.

sections.heading: Grand Junction well drilling cost starts shallow but finishes higher
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in this area, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 20 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $1,000 to $1,500. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,000 to $13,500 at that median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, power distance and site conditions can move the quote. Request a written scope that separates drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, water testing and electrical. The deepest records show why a low median should not be used as a guaranteed price for every Grand Junction parcel.

sections.heading: Environmental and building checks belong in the offer review
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental inventory includes 74 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features and 38 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not automatically make a property unsafe, but they are a reason to identify the proposed well, check the distance to potential sources and obtain current laboratory testing before relying on the water.

Low yield and dry-hole risk also deserve a written discussion, especially because 39% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Confirm septic setbacks, well access for a rig, casing and grout requirements, and the buildable area before finalizing plans. A DWR permit is not a guarantee of water quality, sufficient yield or approval for every intended use. Household-use wells, water rights and any augmentation-plan requirement should be reviewed for the specific parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Grand Junction?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Grand Junction is 20 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 28 feet. About 93% of reported wells are under 100 feet. The records also include wells as deep as 1,690 feet, so neighboring logs are more useful than the median when estimating a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Grand Junction?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 20-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,000 to $1,500. A finished system with a pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,000 to $13,500. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout and power distance can change the actual bid.

faq.q: How much water do Grand Junction wells produce?
faq.a: Among 44 records reporting yield, the median is 5.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 0.1 to 12.6 gallons per minute. Reported results vary widely: 39% are under 1 gallon per minute, while 23% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the individual well test before planning use.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Grand Junction?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Within about 10 miles, records show 74 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features and 38 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the proposed well tested by a qualified laboratory, and check nearby environmental records before buying or relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Grand Junction?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a straightforward decline. Static water levels were 16 feet below surface in the 2000s, 10 feet in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. These measurements come from different wells and conditions, so review actual neighboring logs and recent measurements for the parcel.
